faq.q: Is wild camping legal in Scotland for motorcycle tourers?
faq.a: Yes, under Scotland's Land Reform Act you can wild camp on most unenclosed land. Follow the Outdoor Access Code: camp away from buildings and roads, pitch late and leave early, and take all rubbish with you. This gives motorcycle campers exceptional freedom compared to the rest of Britain.

faq.q: What's the best time of year for motorcycle camping in Scotland?
faq.a: May, June, and September are ideal. May offers spring colours and fewer midges, June gives maximum daylight hours, and September brings autumn colours with emptier roads. July and August are warmest but bring peak midges and tourist crowds.

faq.q: How much luggage space do I need for motorcycle camping in Scotland?
faq.a: You'll need capacity for camping gear (tent, sleeping bag, mat), cooking equipment, clothing for all weathers, and standard touring kit. Most riders use soft panniers plus a 40-50L dry bag on the pillion seat for bulky items like tents and sleeping bags.

faq.q: Where can I find fuel on remote Scottish routes?
faq.a: Fuel stations are scarce in the Highlands, with gaps of 50+ miles on routes like the western NC500. Never pass a pump below half tank. Major refuelling points include Fort William, Ullapool, Durness, Lochinver, and Portree on Skye.

faq.q: Do I need special breakdown cover for Scottish motorcycle camping tours?
faq.a: Yes, ensure your breakdown cover specifically includes the Scottish Highlands and remote single-track roads. Some providers exclude the NC500 or charge extra. Check your policy covers recovery from wild camping locations off main roads.

content:
Why Scotland is the Best Place for Motorcycle Camping in Britain

I've camped across most of Britain on two wheels, and I'll tell you straight: Scotland wins every time. The combination of epic riding roads, wild camping laws, and dramatic landscapes makes it the ultimate destination for motorcycle camping. Whether you're after coastal routes, mountain passes, or remote glens, Scotland delivers in ways that England and Wales simply can't match.

The game-changer here is Scotland's access rights. Under the Land Reform Act, you can wild camp almost anywhere on unenclosed land, as long as you follow the Outdoor Access Code. That means pulling off a quiet track at sunset, pitching up with a view of a loch, and waking to mountains without booking a campsite. I've done this dozens of times, and it transforms how you tour.

But let me be clear: motorcycle camping in Scotland isn't a summer-only activity anymore. In 2026, with improved gear and better forecasting, I'm riding and camping from March through October. Yes, you'll get rain. Yes, it'll be cold some nights. But with the right approach, that's all manageable, and the rewards are absolutely worth it.

The Essential Kit for Scottish Motorcycle Camping

Your gear choices make or break a camping tour. I've learned this through some properly miserable nights in soggy tents and some brilliant ones where everything just worked. Here's what actually matters when you're camping off the bike in Scotland.

Tent Selection and Setup

You need a tent designed for British conditions, which means wind and rain. I run a two-person tent even when solo because you need space for gear. Look for something with a packed size under 50cm and weighing less than 2kg. The Vango Banshee and Wild Country Zephyros are both popular with bike tourers for good reason—they pack small, pitch fast, and handle Scottish weather.

Here's the critical bit: practice pitching it at home before you go. I've watched riders struggle with poles and flysheets in horizontal rain on Skye because they'd never set it up before. Five minutes in your garden saves an hour of misery in the Highlands.

Sleeping System

Your sleeping bag rating matters more in Scotland than anywhere else in Britain. Even in summer, Highland temperatures can drop to 5°C at night. I use a three-season bag rated to -5°C comfort, and I've never regretted carrying the extra bulk. Pair it with a decent inflatable mat—the Thermarest NeoAir or similar. A cheap foam mat will leave you feeling every rock and losing heat to the ground.

Cooking and Food Storage

I've settled on a simple gas canister stove setup. The Jetboil systems are brilliant but bulky. A basic MSR Pocket Rocket or similar gives you hot food and brews without eating luggage space. Carry two gas canisters for a week-long trip—you can usually find them in outdoor shops in Fort William, Ullapool, or Portree, but don't count on it.

For food storage, use a bear-proof bag or stuff sack hung from a tree where possible, mainly to keep foxes and badgers out. I've had curious wildlife investigate my camp more than once, particularly on the West Coast.

Luggage That Actually Works

This is where many riders get it wrong. You need proper weatherproof luggage for Scottish touring. I run soft panniers and a tank bag for camping kit, with my tent and sleeping bag in a dry bag on the pillion seat. Hard luggage works too, but you lose flexibility for the bulkier camping items.

Whatever system you choose, make sure you can access essentials without unpacking everything. I keep my waterproofs, first aid kit, and tool roll in my tank bag—things I might need quickly in changing conditions. Check out SportsBikeShop for luggage options that'll handle Scottish weather.

The Best Routes and Regions for Motorcycle Camping

Scotland offers distinct regions, each with its own character and camping opportunities. I've ridden them all extensively, and here's what you need to know about each.

The North Coast 500

Everyone talks about the NC500, and for good reason. This 516-mile loop from Inverness takes in coastal scenery, mountain passes, and remote single-track roads. For camping, the western section between Durness and Applecross is unbeatable. The Bealach na Bà climb to Applecross is one of Britain's greatest motorcycle roads—switchbacks, gradients up to 20%, and views across to Skye.

For wild camping on the NC500, focus on the quieter sections. The east coast gets busy in summer, but head west past Tongue and you'll find spots where you won't see another person all evening. My favourite wild camp spot is near Clashnessie Bay—park at the small layby, walk 50 metres to a flat spot overlooking the beach, and you've got one of Scotland's best free pitches.

If you're planning the full loop, check out our complete guide on the NC500 route for detailed waypoints and timing.

The Hebrides: Skye, Harris, and Lewis

Island camping is different. You're committed once you're across on the ferry, so weather planning becomes crucial. But the riding is extraordinary. Skye's Trotternish Ridge, the Golden Road on Harris, and the vast emptiness of Lewis offer experiences you can't get on the mainland.

For camping, head to Glenbrittle on Skye for a campsite with direct access to the Cuillin mountains, or wild camp on Harris near Luskentyre Beach—it's consistently rated one of Britain's best beaches. The wind can be savage on the islands, so guy your tent properly and use extra pegs. I carry an additional eight lightweight pegs specifically for exposed sites.

The ferry to Skye from Mallaig or the crossing to Harris from Uig requires booking ahead in summer. Plan this before you leave—there's nothing worse than riding to a ferry and finding you're waiting 12 hours for the next sailing.

The Cairngorms and Central Highlands

This region offers the most varied riding and camping. The A939 Cockbridge to Tomintoul road is Britain's highest main route and usually the first to close in winter. Ride it in May or September for the best conditions—clear days, autumn colours, and minimal traffic.

For camping, Glen Etive is a personal favourite. It's off the A82 south of Glen Coe, a single-track road that runs deep into the mountains. Wild camping is established here, with multiple spots along the river. You're close enough to civilisation for a pub meal in Glen Coe village but remote enough to feel properly wild.

The A93 through Glen Shee and the A939 through Glenshee both offer brilliant riding with camping opportunities at Braemar or wild spots in the glens. This is red deer country, so you'll likely see wildlife, especially at dawn and dusk.

The Borders and Southern Scotland

Often overlooked, the Borders offer excellent motorcycle camping without the crowds. The A708 through Moffat Dale and the minor roads around St Mary's Loch are genuinely brilliant riding roads—technical, flowing, and scenic.

For camping, the Galloway Forest Park has several campsites, or wild camp near Loch Trool. This is dark sky territory, so on clear nights you'll get star views that rival the Highlands. The riding is more wooded and intimate than the Highlands, with better weather odds if you're touring in April or October.

Scottish Weather and When to Ride

Let's be honest about Scottish weather: it's changeable, often wet, and can catch you out. But it's not the constant rain that riders fear. I've had week-long trips in June with wall-to-wall sunshine and August weekends where it rained every day. The key is accepting you'll get some rain and preparing accordingly.

The best months for motorcycle camping in Scotland are May, June, and September. May gives you longer days, spring colours, and fewer midges. June is peak daylight—you can ride until 10 pm in the far north—but it's also peak tourist season on popular routes. September offers autumn colours, clearer air, and emptier roads, though nights get cold quickly.

July and August are warmest but bring midges and crowds. The midges are genuine torture in still conditions near water—I've abandoned camps because of them. Carry midge repellent with DEET or Saltidin, and camp on exposed spots where wind keeps them away.

The single best weather decision you can make is flexibility. Don't commit to a fixed itinerary—follow the weather forecast and adjust your route daily. If rain is forecast for the west, head east. If it's blowing a gale on the NC500, explore inland glens instead.

Wild Camping vs Campsites: Making the Choice

Both have their place in a Scottish motorcycle tour. I typically mix them—wild camping for the experience and freedom, campsites when I want a hot shower and the chance to dry gear properly.

Wild Camping Essentials

When wild camping, follow the Outdoor Access Code strictly. This means camping away from buildings, roads, and other people where possible. Pitch late and leave early—I usually arrive after 7 pm and leave by 10 am. Take all rubbish with you, bury toilet waste properly, and use existing fire rings if you're having a fire (though I rarely bother with fires when motorcycle camping—too much hassle).

The best wild camping spots are those you find yourself, but here are some proven areas: the shore of Loch Morlich in the Cairngorms, various spots along Glen Etive, near Sanna Bay on the Ardnamurchan Peninsula, and around the lochs in Assynt. Use OS Maps on your phone to identify flat ground near water but away from obvious camping spots that attract crowds.

Recommended Campsites

For proper facilities, these campsites are all motorcycle-friendly and well-located for touring:

  • Sango Sands, Durness—stunning beach location, perfect for the NC500
  • Glenbrittle, Skye—basic facilities but incredible mountain setting
  • Rothiemurchus Camp, Aviemore—good central base with all facilities
  • Glen Nevis, Fort William—can be busy but excellent location
  • Glencoe Mountain, Glen Coe—purpose-built for outdoor enthusiasts

Most charge £10-15 per person for tent camping, with hot showers included. Many now offer electric hook-ups if you're running heated gear or need to charge devices.

Safety and Practical Considerations

Motorcycle camping in Scotland requires more planning than a simple camping trip or a regular bike tour. You're combining the challenges of both, often in remote locations with limited mobile coverage.

Communication and Navigation

Mobile signal is patchy across the Highlands. I carry an OS map as backup and download offline maps to my phone. Tell someone your rough plan and expected return date—basic stuff, but it matters when you're camping in remote glens.

Use our route builder tool to plan your daily distances with camping spots marked. I aim for 100-150 miles per day when camping—enough to see brilliant roads but leaving time to set up camp properly before dark.

Fuel and Supplies

Fuel stations are scarce in the Highlands. Never pass a pump below half a tank—genuinely. The gaps between stations can be 50+ miles on some routes, and running out is not only embarrassing but potentially dangerous.

The same goes for food supplies. Stock up in larger towns like Fort William, Ullapool, or Portree. Small village shops exist but have limited supplies and shorter hours. I carry two days of emergency food (pasta, packet noodles, energy bars) that stays in my luggage regardless.

Breakdown and Recovery

Make sure your breakdown cover includes Scotland and specifically the Highlands. Some providers exclude the NC500 or charge extra for recovery from remote single-track roads. BMW Motorrad Assistance and RAC both cover remote Scottish roads, but check your specific policy.

Carry basic tools and know how to use them. I've fixed punctures, adjusted chains, and replaced fuses on Scottish roadsides. A puncture repair kit is essential—the nearest tyre replacement could be 100 miles away.

Making the Most of Your Scottish Camping Tour

The technical stuff matters, but don't let it overshadow the experience. Scottish motorcycle camping is about moments: that first proper view of the mountains as you ride north from Perth, a sunrise over a loch from your tent, or the satisfaction of a challenging road ridden well in changeable conditions.

Take time to stop and explore off the bike. Some of Scotland's best experiences aren't from the saddle—walking to remote beaches, visiting distilleries, or simply sitting by your tent with a brew watching the light change on the mountains. I often build rest days into longer tours, setting up base camp and riding out on day trips without luggage.

Connect with other riders. The motorcycle touring community in Scotland is welcoming. You'll meet fellow tourers at campsites, viewpoints, and fuel stops. Share route tips, weather information, and stories. Some of my best route discoveries came from conversations in petrol station car parks.

If you're new to motorcycle camping, start with a short trip. The Island to Highlands route makes an excellent first tour—three to four days, mixing camping with accessible roads and facilities. Build your experience before tackling longer, more remote tours.

Your Next Steps

Right, you've got the information. Now it's about making it happen. Start by checking your gear—what do you have, what do you need? Use our packing checklist to ensure you're not forgetting essentials.

Book your time off work. Seriously, do it now. The best intentions fail without dates in the diary. Aim for at least four days for your first proper motorcycle camping trip in Scotland—one travel day each end and two full days exploring.

Choose your route based on your experience level. If you're new to Scottish riding, stick to the main A roads and established routes initially. The NC500 is popular for good reason, but also consider lesser-known areas like the Borders or Dumfries and Galloway for your first trip—they're more forgiving and less remote.

Then get out there. Scottish motorcycle camping is genuinely one of Britain's best riding experiences. The combination of brilliant roads, camping freedom, and stunning scenery creates trips you'll remember for years. I've been touring Scotland for over a decade, and I'm still finding new routes and wild camp spots that surprise me.

The weather will challenge you. The midges will annoy you. But when you're sitting outside your tent at 9 pm with a brew, watching the sun set over the Hebrides after a day of perfect riding, you'll understand exactly why Scotland is worth every mile.
